notes.D: The vestibulo-ocular reflex stabilises gaze during head movement and is unrelated to cervical stretch-induced uterine contraction.

questions.stem: Which mediator is especially involved in cervical softening and ripening near delivery?
questions.why: Prostaglandin E2 promotes cervical ripening through local extracellular matrix remodelling, altered collagen organisation and increased tissue hydration. These changes soften the cervix and facilitate dilation; prostaglandin signalling also participates in uterine contractile activation during labour.

notes.B: TSH stimulates thyroid hormone production and does not directly mediate the local cervical matrix remodelling characteristic of labour preparation.
notes.C: Glucagon supports circulating glucose availability through hepatic metabolic effects rather than promoting cervical softening and extracellular matrix reorganisation.
notes.D: Parathyroid hormone regulates calcium and phosphate balance, rather than serving as the characteristic mediator of cervical ripening near term.
notes.E: Vasopressin regulates water conservation and vascular tone, rather than providing the principal prostaglandin-mediated cervical remodelling signal.

questions.stem: Increasing gap junctions between myometrial cells near term have what functional consequence?

options.label: C
options.text: Loss of all uterine electrical coupling

questions.why: Increased myometrial gap junction formation, particularly involving connexin 43, allows ionic current to pass between adjacent smooth-muscle cells. Electrical coupling promotes spread of depolarisation and coordinated uterine contractions instead of independent local muscle activity.

notes.A: Greater intercellular electrical coupling favours synchronisation rather than increasing the isolation of individual myometrial cell contractions.
notes.C: Gap junction channels provide direct electrical communication between neighbouring cells, so increased expression enhances rather than abolishes electrical coupling.
notes.D: Coordinated depolarisation supports calcium-dependent contraction; increased gap junction formation does not directly suppress all intracellular calcium elevation.
notes.E: Oxytocin can stimulate myometrial contraction alongside gap junction-mediated coordination; enhanced coupling does not completely block its receptor-mediated action.

questions.stem: Which stimulus provides a mechanical contribution to the initiation and reinforcement of labour?

options.label: C
options.text: Distension of the uterus and cervix

questions.why: Uterine enlargement and mechanical stretch can increase myometrial excitability and expression of contraction-associated proteins. Cervical distension from the presenting fetal part additionally recruits neuroendocrine feedback that helps reinforce labour, alongside hormonal and inflammatory signals.

notes.A: Reduced uterine stretch would remove a mechanical stimulus rather than explain increased contraction-associated signalling near the onset of labour.
notes.B: Decreased pressure on the cervix reduces stimulation of stretch-sensitive afferents, rather than reinforcing the Ferguson reflex during labour.
notes.D: Suppression of cervical sensory input would weaken the positive-feedback pathway linking cervical stretch to increased oxytocin-mediated uterine contractions.
notes.E: Calcium availability is essential for myometrial smooth-muscle contraction; complete loss of intracellular calcium would impair rather than initiate labour contractions.

questions.stem: What principally distinguishes prolactin from oxytocin in breastfeeding?
questions.why: Prolactin acts on mammary secretory epithelial cells to support synthesis of milk components, whereas oxytocin contracts surrounding myoepithelial cells to expel stored milk. These distinct endocrine responses coordinate production and transfer of milk during suckling.

notes.A: This reverses the two hormone functions: prolactin promotes milk synthesis, while oxytocin produces myoepithelial contraction and milk ejection.
notes.B: Ductal growth and contraction are not the principal contrast; the key distinction concerns milk production versus mechanical release of existing milk.
notes.C: Colostrum digestion and uptake occur in the infant rather than defining the respective maternal endocrine actions of prolactin and oxytocin.
notes.E: Oocyte maturation and release depend principally on ovarian gonadotropin signalling, rather than the two hormones coordinating lactation.

questions.stem: A mother has adequate prolactin but poor milk removal from the breast. What can eventually happen?
questions.why: Milk accumulation increases local intramammary pressure and engages autocrine and paracrine inhibitory mechanisms that reduce milk synthesis. Therefore, adequate prolactin alone cannot sustain maximal supply if milk is repeatedly retained rather than effectively removed.

notes.A: Persistent milk retention generally inhibits further synthesis rather than continuously accelerating secretion despite increasing fullness of the breast.
notes.B: Reduced milk removal can suppress synthesis locally without requiring complete loss of mammary progesterone receptors.
notes.C: Milk stasis results from inadequate drainage and does not automatically resolve simply because prolactin concentrations are adequate.
notes.D: Continued inefficient removal tends to downregulate milk production, rather than producing a permanent increase in supply regardless of demand.

questions.stem: What term describes the established phase of lactation maintained by ongoing milk removal?
questions.why: Galactopoiesis describes maintenance of established milk secretion after secretory activation. Continued effective milk removal, local feedback mechanisms and adequate endocrine support sustain production, adapting supply to the amount of milk regularly transferred or expressed.

notes.B: Lactogenesis I describes secretory differentiation during pregnancy, before the established demand-responsive phase of copious milk production after birth.
notes.C: Implantation and decidualisation prepare the uterine environment for pregnancy, rather than describing the maintenance of mammary milk secretion.
notes.D: Follicular recruitment involves ovarian follicle development during reproductive cycles, not local regulation of established mammary milk production.
notes.E: Luteolysis denotes regression of the corpus luteum, rather than the maintenance phase of lactation following its initial secretory activation.

questions.stem: Why do milk volumes rise sharply after placental delivery?
questions.why: Delivery of the placenta rapidly removes a major source of progesterone, relieving its inhibition of copious mammary milk secretion. In the presence of prolactin and other supportive hormones, this triggers postpartum secretory activation and increasing milk volume.

notes.A: Placental hCG declines after delivery as trophoblastic tissue is removed, rather than rising to trigger copious postpartum milk production.
notes.C: Prolactin remains essential for milk synthesis, so its disappearance would impair rather than explain the activation of abundant milk secretion.
notes.D: Oxytocin supports milk ejection during suckling and is not absent after delivery; progesterone withdrawal chiefly enables increased synthesis.
notes.E: Inhibin regulates pituitary FSH and does not provide the main endocrine trigger of secretory activation after placental delivery.

questions.stem: Frequent exclusive suckling can delay ovulation by reducing which hypothalamic signal?
questions.why: Frequent suckling modifies hypothalamic reproductive signalling and suppresses pulsatile GnRH release, partly through prolactin-related pathways. Reduced gonadotropin support can delay follicular maturation and ovulation, although the duration and contraceptive reliability of lactational amenorrhoea vary.

notes.A: TRH regulates thyroid-stimulating hormone and can influence prolactin, but suppression of pulsatile GnRH is the central reproductive mechanism described.
notes.B: CRH participates in the stress axis regulating ACTH secretion, rather than being the principal hypothalamic signal whose suppression delays ovulation during lactation.
notes.D: GHRH stimulates growth hormone secretion and does not directly provide the essential pulsatile gonadotropin drive required for normal ovarian ovulation.
notes.E: Vasopressin regulates water balance through posterior pituitary release, rather than controlling follicular maturation through the hypothalamic–pituitary–gonadal axis.

questions.stem: Which sensory event starts the neuroendocrine milk-ejection reflex?
questions.why: Mechanical stimulation of the nipple during suckling activates sensory afferents projecting through spinal and hypothalamic pathways. Magnocellular oxytocin neurons increase hormone release from the posterior pituitary, causing mammary myoepithelial contraction and milk ejection.

notes.A: Follicular rupture releases an ovarian oocyte and does not provide the sensory input initiating the mammary milk-ejection reflex.
notes.B: Carotid sinus stretch activates cardiovascular baroreflex pathways, rather than the nipple-associated sensory signals responsible for oxytocin-mediated milk let-down.
notes.C: Intestinal nutrient absorption supplies maternal metabolic substrates but does not constitute the immediate sensory trigger of milk ejection during suckling.
notes.E: Renal sodium transport regulates electrolyte and fluid balance, rather than providing afferent signals that initiate the mammary neuroendocrine reflex.

questions.stem: Which event is most likely to acutely interrupt milk let-down despite adequate milk production?
questions.why: Acute stress can interfere with hypothalamic oxytocin release or the coordinated milk-ejection response. Consequently, milk may already be present within mammary alveoli but fail to flow effectively until the neuroendocrine let-down response is restored.

notes.A: Increased prolactin receptor availability generally supports mammary responsiveness for milk synthesis rather than acutely interrupting oxytocin-mediated ejection.
notes.B: Increased milk synthesis may increase available milk volume, but does not itself explain failure of the neuroendocrine milk-ejection response.
notes.C: Hepatic glucose production supports metabolic fuel availability and is not the specific central mechanism blocking milk let-down despite adequate supply.
notes.D: Ovarian inhibin regulates pituitary FSH secretion and is not the principal acute inhibitor of the mammary oxytocin reflex.

questions.stem: The lobuloalveolar structures of the breast grow extensively during pregnancy under which hormones?
questions.why: Oestrogen promotes mammary ductal expansion, while progesterone particularly supports lobular and alveolar growth during pregnancy. Together with prolactin, placental lactogen and other endocrine signals, these ovarian and placental steroids prepare mammary tissue for postpartum milk production.

notes.B: Prolactin supports secretory differentiation and oxytocin mediates ejection, but oestrogen and progesterone are the principal steroid pair driving extensive structural development.
notes.C: Cortisol provides permissive metabolic support, while aldosterone regulates fluid and electrolytes; neither pair principally explains pregnancy-associated mammary structural expansion.
notes.D: Thyroxine and calcitriol support systemic metabolic and mineral physiology, rather than forming the major reproductive steroid combination driving mammary development.
notes.E: Gonadotropins regulate gonadal activity and inhibin feedback, rather than directly replacing the pregnancy-associated oestrogen and progesterone effects on mammary tissue.

questions.stem: What fetal vessel is most directly surrounded by maternal blood in the placental intervillous space?
questions.why: Fetal capillaries run inside chorionic villi projecting into maternal blood-filled intervillous spaces. Maternal blood bathes the trophoblastic surface rather than directly contacting fetal endothelium, permitting exchange across the intervening placental barrier.

notes.A: Maternal spiral arteries deliver maternal blood into intervillous spaces and are not the fetal vessels lying within chorionic villous cores.
notes.C: Maternal venous channels drain intervillous blood, rather than carrying fetal blood within placental exchange villi.
notes.D: The umbilical vein carries oxygenated fetal blood away from the placenta but lies outside the intervillous exchange region described.
notes.E: Maternal uterine lymphatic vessels drain tissue fluid and do not constitute the fetal capillary circulation within placental chorionic villi.

questions.stem: Maternal-fetal transfer of oxygen is mainly driven by what?
questions.why: Oxygen diffuses down its partial-pressure gradient across the placenta.

questions.stem: Which vessel carries comparatively oxygenated blood from the placenta toward the fetal liver?
questions.why: One umbilical vein returns oxygenated placental blood to the fetus.

questions.stem: Which vessels convey fetal blood toward the placenta for oxygenation?
questions.why: Paired umbilical arteries return comparatively deoxygenated blood to the placenta.

questions.stem: The ductus venosus directs part of umbilical venous blood into which vessel?
questions.why: The ductus venosus bypasses part of the liver and joins the inferior vena cava.

questions.stem: What is the main direction of blood movement through the fetal foramen ovale?
questions.why: The foramen ovale permits right-to-left atrial shunting before birth.

questions.stem: Which fetal channel connects the pulmonary artery to the descending aorta?
questions.why: The ductus arteriosus shunts blood away from high-resistance fetal lungs.

questions.stem: Why is pulmonary blood flow relatively low in the fetus?
questions.why: Fluid-filled, unventilated fetal lungs maintain high pulmonary vascular resistance.

questions.stem: What makes placental circulation a major low-resistance component of fetal systemic flow?

options.label: C
options.text: Complete lack of fetal cardiac output

questions.why: The placental circulation forms a low-resistance pathway in fetal circulation.

questions.stem: Why is oxygenated blood from the ductus venosus preferentially directed toward the fetal brain and heart?

options.label: C
options.text: Shunting from aorta to vena cava

questions.why: Streaming of inferior vena caval blood across the foramen ovale favors supply to the left heart.

questions.stem: Why do fetal ventricles function more in parallel than in series?

options.label: A
options.text: Only the left ventricle pumps blood

options.label: C
options.text: Only the right ventricle pumps blood

options.label: D
options.text: All blood must cross the lungs

questions.why: Fetal shunts distribute combined ventricular output to the systemic and placental circulations.

questions.stem: Which fetal chamber pumps most of its output into the ductus arteriosus?
questions.why: High pulmonary resistance diverts much right ventricular output through the ductus arteriosus.

questions.stem: The first effective breaths rapidly lower pulmonary vascular resistance mainly through what?
questions.why: Aeration and higher alveolar oxygen dilate pulmonary vessels.

questions.stem: Clamping the umbilical cord normally causes which immediate systemic change?
questions.why: Removal of low-resistance placental circulation raises systemic vascular resistance.

questions.stem: Functional closure of the foramen ovale follows which pressure relationship?
questions.why: Increased pulmonary venous return raises left atrial pressure and opposes right-to-left shunting.

questions.stem: Why does the ductus arteriosus constrict after a healthy term birth?
questions.why: Increased arterial oxygen and falling prostaglandins favor ductal constriction.

questions.stem: Which adult anatomical remnant derives from the ductus arteriosus?
questions.why: The ductus arteriosus becomes the ligamentum arteriosum.

questions.stem: Which adult structure marks the closed fetal foramen ovale?
questions.why: Fusion of the atrial septal flap leaves the fossa ovalis.

questions.stem: Which adult remnant corresponds to the former ductus venosus?
questions.why: The ductus venosus becomes the ligamentum venosum in the liver.

questions.stem: After birth, the umbilical vein normally forms which hepatic structure?
questions.why: The remnant of the left umbilical vein is the round ligament of the liver.

questions.stem: Premature neonates are especially vulnerable to alveolar collapse mainly because of low levels of what?
questions.why: Type II pneumocyte surfactant reduces alveolar surface tension and prevents atelectasis.

questions.stem: Which lung cell is responsible for synthesis and secretion of pulmonary surfactant?
questions.why: Type II alveolar cells produce surfactant.

questions.stem: Successful clearance of fetal lung liquid at birth relies importantly on increased what?
questions.why: Birth-related epithelial sodium transport helps remove fluid from the airspaces.

questions.stem: What is the principal effect of pulmonary surfactant during the newborn's first breaths?
questions.why: Surfactant reduces the pressure needed to inflate small alveoli.

questions.stem: Why are preterm babies prone to hypoglycaemia shortly after birth?
questions.why: Limited glycogen and fat stores plus immature glucose production increase vulnerability.

questions.stem: Newborn infants generate heat without shivering predominantly by oxidizing what tissue?
questions.why: Brown fat supports nonshivering thermogenesis through mitochondrial uncoupling.

questions.stem: Which mitochondrial protein enables heat generation in neonatal brown adipose tissue?
questions.why: UCP1 dissipates the proton gradient as heat instead of conserving it as ATP.

questions.stem: Physiological neonatal jaundice is partly related to immaturity of which liver process?
questions.why: Immature UGT-mediated conjugation reduces bilirubin clearance in the newborn.

questions.stem: Why is vitamin K prophylaxis important soon after birth?

options.label: A
options.text: Excess vitamin K from placental blood

options.label: E
options.text: Low stores and limited gut vitamin K

questions.why: Neonates have limited vitamin K reserves and immature intestinal flora.

questions.stem: Which renal feature makes young neonates more vulnerable to fluid imbalance?

options.label: A
options.text: Low GFR and limited concentrating ability

questions.why: Immature filtration and tubular function limit neonatal water and solute regulation.

questions.stem: Why is severe neonatal bradycardia especially likely to depress cardiac output?

options.label: A
options.text: Excess ability to increase stroke volume

options.label: B
options.text: Limited ability to raise stroke volume

questions.why: The neonatal heart is relatively heart-rate dependent because stroke volume reserve is limited.

questions.stem: Fetal haemoglobin has reduced affinity for which red-cell regulator compared with adult Hb?
questions.why: HbF binds 2,3-BPG less strongly, helping it acquire oxygen at placental tensions.

questions.stem: What happens to the predominant haemoglobin composition after the neonatal period?
questions.why: Gamma-chain synthesis declines while beta-chain-containing adult Hb rises after birth.

questions.stem: A newborn with persistent high pulmonary resistance continues a right-to-left ductal shunt. Which condition does this describe?
questions.why: Persistent pulmonary hypertension maintains high PVR and can preserve fetal right-to-left shunting.

questions.stem: Which clinical change most often marks the beginning of normal male puberty?
questions.why: Testicular enlargement is typically the earliest clear sign of male puberty.

questions.stem: Kisspeptin signalling at puberty chiefly increases secretion of which hypothalamic hormone?
questions.why: Kisspeptin activates GnRH neurons and helps initiate pulsatile gonadotropin secretion.

questions.stem: A 14-year-old boy has no increase in testicular size. This most strongly suggests what?
questions.why: Lack of testicular enlargement by 14 warrants evaluation for delayed puberty.

questions.stem: A genetic male with deficient five-alpha reductase may develop ambiguous external genitalia because which hormone is deficient locally?
questions.why: DHT supports development of male external genitalia during fetal life.

questions.stem: Which androgen is particularly important for development of the male internal Wolffian ducts?
questions.why: Testosterone supports Wolffian duct derivatives, while DHT chiefly masculinizes external genitalia.

questions.stem: What mechanical process helps maintain an erection after cavernosal smooth muscle relaxes?
questions.why: Expanding sinusoids compress emissary veins against the tunica albuginea.

questions.stem: Increased sympathetic alpha-adrenergic activity terminates erection primarily by what?
questions.why: Alpha-adrenergic contraction reduces arterial inflow and restores venous drainage.

questions.stem: A boy with severe testosterone deficiency before puberty may develop which finding?
questions.why: Without adequate testosterone the expected pubertal masculine changes are blunted.

questions.stem: Which event is commonly the first visible sign of female puberty?
questions.why: Thelarche generally precedes pubic hair maturation and menarche.

questions.stem: Pulsatile rather than continuous GnRH signalling is physiologically necessary mainly to maintain what?
questions.why: Pulsatile GnRH sustains gonadotropin secretion; continuous exposure desensitizes the system.

questions.stem: What is the conventional clinical definition of natural menopause?
questions.why: Natural menopause is diagnosed retrospectively after 12 consecutive months of amenorrhoea without another cause.

questions.stem: A menopausal woman's vasomotor hot flushes are principally associated with what endocrine transition?

options.label: A
options.text: Rapid rise in corpus luteum progesterone

questions.why: Follicle depletion lowers estrogen and affects central temperature regulation.

questions.stem: Why does ovulation cease in natural menopause despite elevated FSH?
questions.why: Loss of the follicular pool prevents effective ovarian response to high gonadotropins.

questions.stem: Which sequence represents the conventional four-phase human sexual response model?
questions.why: The EPOR model comprises excitement, plateau, orgasm and resolution.

questions.stem: Which autonomic mechanism contributes importantly to genital vasocongestion during arousal?
questions.why: Parasympathetic vasodilatation increases genital blood flow during arousal.

questions.stem: Vaginal lubrication during arousal arises substantially from which process?
questions.why: Increased genital blood flow causes plasma transudation across vaginal mucosa.

questions.stem: The resolution phase of the sexual response cycle is best characterized by what?

options.label: B
options.text: Return of genital blood flow toward baseline

questions.why: Resolution follows orgasm or cessation of stimulation with return toward resting physiology.
